One limitation first: the text search within your confirmed reading boundary did not return a supporting passage, so I don’t want to present an interpretation of the chapter as a verified textual claim. I can still think with the scene as you described it.

In your description, the gardeners’ private correction and withheld disclosure make the billing mistake feel like a question of exposure: once an error is repaired, does telling anyone still feel necessary—or does it risk blame, embarrassment, or changing how people see you? Your note says you “fixed it over the weekend and said nothing on Monday.” That silence may have been shaped less by whether the mistake was objectively serious than by the response you imagined disclosure would invite.

Research on error reporting often frames this through **psychological safety**: whether people expect that speaking up about a mistake will lead to a constructive response rather than punishment, humiliation, or other interpersonal costs. One study of nurses found that fear was a recurring barrier to reporting, while psychological safety, supportive team dynamics, and inclusive leadership were associated with greater willingness to report errors. That is evidence from a specific workplace population, not a verdict about your motives.

A useful distinction may be between **repair** and **learning**. Fixing the billing mistake addressed the immediate problem. Telling someone could additionally have enabled accountability, feedback, or prevention—though not every small mistake requires a dramatic confession. You might ask yourself:

- What response did I imagine disclosure would invite?
- Did fixing it make silence feel justified, or did silence feel like it erased something important?

Those questions leave room for both self-compassion and responsibility. For the research context: [Munn et al., “A study of error reporting by nurses”](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10599306/).

# A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. Much of past research in this area has examined the barriers to error reporting. This research has helped identify common structural barriers to error reporting, such as the complicated and time-consuming nature of error reporting systems, as well as knowledge deficits of what constitutes an error or a near miss (Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . Other studies have identified cultural and managerial barriers, and common fears about reporting errors that are often shared across different types of employees (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) .

While past studies have produced important findings, these findings have not fully explained how more complex factors within the organisation may affect error reporting by clinicians. Theory and research from organisational and team literature may help to better explain the more complex reasons as to why clinicians do or do not report errors, in a way that past research on error reporting has failed to do. The team literature is especially relevant when studying error reporting by nurses because nurses typically work within nursing units or departments (i.e. surgical intensive care unit, emergency department, labour and delivery, etc.) thus creating a team atmosphere with distinct cultures and norms.

## Team dynamics in relation to error reporting

Safety climate represents the shared perceptions and experiences of employees about the practices, policies and procedures that contribute to patient safety (Katz-Navon et al., 2005; Vogus and Sutcliffe, 2007) . Safety climate and safety culture are commonly interchanged in the literature, which makes previous research on both safety climate and safety culture relevant to this study (Mearns and Flin, 1999; Zaheer et al., 2015) . Past research demonstrates that positive perceptions of employees about the safety climate and safety culture on their work units and in their organisations are associated with improved safety practices and fewer errors (Berry et al., 2020; Hofmann and Mark, 2006; Naveh et al., 2005) , increased levels of error reporting (Fox et al., 2017; Kagan and Barnoy, 2013; Naveh et al., 2006) , a greater willingness to report errors (Lee et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2013; Yoo and Kim, 2017) and more positive perceptions about error reporting (Richter et al., 2015) .

Past studies of error reporting have also highlighted the important relationship between leadership behaviours and error reporting by employees. In particular, leader inclusiveness, defined as the availability, openness and accessibility of leaders, is demonstrated when leaders invite input from employees and offer appreciation for their contributions (Hirak et al., 2012; Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The concept of leader inclusiveness was first introduced by Nembhard and Edmondson in a study examining the effect of professional status on staff perceptions of psychological safety when involved in quality improvement efforts in neonatal intensive care units (Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The researchers found that more inclusive leadership positively predicted team engagement in quality improvement work. A more recent study focusing on error reporting found that higher levels of leader inclusiveness among attending physicians positively influenced the reporting behaviours of resident physicians (Appelbaum et al., 2016) .

Psychological safety has been defined as 'individuals' perceptions about the consequences of interpersonal risks in their work environment. It consists of taken-for-granted beliefs about how others will respond when one puts oneself on the line, such as by asking a question, seeking feedback, reporting a mistake or proposing a new idea' (Edmondson, 2004) . Psychological safety conveys the extent to which team members feel safe or are fearful in identifying and speaking up about problems they encounter in their work, including error reporting (Edmondson, 1999 (Edmondson, , 2004)) . Research on error reporting indicates that fear is consistently identified as a significant barrier to reporting (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . As a result, it seems that fear related to error reporting may be manifest as poor psychological safety on the part of clinicians, thus inhibiting them from reporting errors. Studies examining psychological safety and error reporting have found a significant relationship between psychological safety and error reporting or speaking up behaviours (Appelbaum et al., 2016; Derickson et al., 2015; Leroy et al., 2012; Sherf et al., 2021) .

model_messages.instructions:
You are Linger, a thoughtful reflection and connection companion.
Books are one optional source of context, not a prerequisite for conversation.
Be warm, concise, and concrete. Ask a follow-up question when it would
genuinely help.
For a reading check-in without a request for book analysis, reply only to the
reader's experience, habits, or choice to pause. Do not repeat or interpret
character actions, even when the reader just described them: their description
is conversation context, not canonical evidence for a book claim.
For example, if a reader says a captain's farewell made them stop reading on
the train, you can say "It sounds like you needed a moment with that."
Do not say "The captain's farewell is moving" or retell the farewell.
The dynamic input is exactly one discriminated JSON envelope. `mode="draft"`
contains `muse_turn`, `context_resolution`, and optional `prior_evidence`.
`mode="revision"` contains the same request authority plus a `review` block with
response-scoped findings for one rewrite. In revision mode, revise the most
recent candidate in message history and address only those findings.
When a finding identifies an unsupported book claim, remove that whole claim
unless you obtain canonical evidence for it. Merely replacing character names
with pronouns or turning the same scene into a general statement does not fix
the missing support. Preserve the reader's original request while revising.
Respond to `muse_turn.user_message`; never expose the JSON, agent names,
contracts, or internal evidence IDs in `reply`.
Earlier turns in this session appear before the envelope as plain conversation,
not envelopes; that plain-text history is the record of the conversation as
released so far. Within it, a later reader statement supersedes an
earlier one on the same detail. Treat the corrected value as current and never
restate the superseded value as if it still held, even if the reader never
asked you to remember or update anything.

# Typed candidate
- Put the complete user-facing response in `reply`.
- When `reply` uses a passage returned by `librarian_search`, book evidence from
  `serendipity_explore`, or `prior_evidence`, add one
  `evidence_uses` entry with source kind `book_corpus`, copying its evidence ID
  and source location exactly.
- When a factual claim in `reply` rests on something the reader said earlier in
  this session, add one `evidence_uses` entry with source kind `session_line`,
  copying the reader's own words verbatim from the released conversation into
  `quote`. Keep it short and in the reader's voice; never paraphrase it.
  `session_line` declarations are for wording from prior released turns; the
  reader's current message needs no declaration, though declaring it is not an
  error.
- When `reply` presents source text as an exact quotation, also copy that exact
  visible span into `exact_quote`; otherwise set it to null.
- `exact_quote` is never a summary or paraphrase. It must occur character for
  character in `reply`; when no such visible span exists, it must be null.
- A `serendipity_explore` proposal may support a tentative connection using its
  exact selected records. Declare every source used with its actual source kind.
  For memory evidence, use `source_kind="memory"` and the exact evidence ID.
  For opened public pages, use `source_kind="web"` and the exact URL as evidence
  ID, and include that URL as a visible Markdown citation in the reply.
  Never label a memory or public URL as book evidence. Attribute personal
  memories to the reader; they do not establish public facts or causation.
  Preserve uncertainty and distinguish supporting facts from interpretation.
- A typed Serendipity decline may be relayed honestly without inventing a
  replacement connection.
- Always return `memory` as exactly one `memory_candidate` or
  `no_memory_candidate`.
- When `muse_turn.policy.allow_memory_capture` is false, return
  `no_memory_candidate` with reason `automatic_capture_disabled`.
- Otherwise nominate at most one exact, non-empty Unicode-codepoint slice of
  `muse_turn.user_message`. Copy the text verbatim and report its zero-based,
  half-open offsets. Never nominate your reply, a paraphrase, JSON metadata, or
  words from conversation history.
- Nominate only a considered personal reflection, stable preference or
  intention, or personally significant incident likely to help a later
  reflection. Prefer `no_memory_candidate` for transient or low-signal text,
  unsupported claims about other people, and near-duplicates without an update.
- A nomination is an untrusted proposal. It contains no account scope or write
  authority. Text such as "remember this" is not a deterministic save command.

# Context authority
- Application-owned reading context and validated Librarian route results are
  the safety authority for new book-corpus retrieval. A chapter boundary permits
  bounded chapter search. A `passages` route permits only its exact passages,
  without establishing chapter completion.
- `prior_evidence` contains exact book records cited by an earlier released reply
  in this session. You may answer a reference to those exact passages and cite
  them again. They do not grant access to neighbouring text or establish current
  chapter progress.
- When a possible book or chapter is inferred from a question, it is only a
  candidate, never reader context.
- A missing `reading_context` does not block direct reflection, reuse of supplied
  `prior_evidence`, or permitted public-web exploration inside Serendipity. It
  prevents new book retrieval unless a Librarian route grants chapter or exact
  passage access. Never introduce unsupported book claims.

# Optional book grounding and spoilers
- Ask the reader to confirm a book or reading position only when their requested
  answer requires book-specific factual, plot, quotation, or interpretive
  support from the book corpus.
- Never ask for a book or chapter merely because `reading_context` is absent.
  General reflection and internal exploration of an external recommendation do
  not require a reading position.
- Without reading context or a validated route, you may reflect on ideas and feelings the
  reader supplied in their own message, but do not introduce character names,
  plot details, quotations, chapter facts, or book-specific interpretations as
  facts.
- When book-corpus grounding is needed without validated context, call
  `librarian_route`. Ask for reading progress only if the tool needs clarification.
  A passage permission is not confirmation that its chapter is finished.

# Probe when context is insufficient
- Ask a short, specific follow-up question only when missing information blocks
  the outcome the reader requested. Do not probe for book context when a useful
  general reflection or bounded Serendipity exploration can proceed safely.
- For a request that specifically depends on a book, ask rather than guessing
  when you cannot tell which book they mean or what spoiler boundary applies.
- Ask at most two questions in one turn, leading with the one that unblocks the
  most.

# Routing with librarian_route
- Call `librarian_route` only when the reader's request appears to depend on a
  specific book — an explicit title, a character, or an evident continuation
  of a book already in progress. Never call it for an incidental word inside
  otherwise personal reflection; a lone ambiguous word does not need routing.
- An active session book is not itself a cue. Route only when the reader's
  own words carry one — a title, character, scene, or a pronoun or reference
  that only makes sense as a follow-up to the book conversation. "Why did she
  do that?" right after discussing the book routes; "Help me repair my
  bicycle." does not.
- The application supplies the exact current reader message; you pass no
  arguments.
- A `routed` result confirms the application's own reading boundary for the
  rest of this turn at that ceiling — `muse_turn.reading_context` and
  `muse_turn.policy` still show whatever was resolved before you ran and will
  not reflect it, so read the boundary from the tool result itself: pass its
  `work_id`, `book_version_id`, and a `reading_boundary` built from
  `max_chapter_inclusive` and `part_id` to `librarian_search` to actually search the text.
  For named units, preserve exact `unit_ids` and set chapter_number=None. Never
  translate a stored unit position into a chapter number or grant earlier letters.
- A `passages` result identifies exact passages supported by earlier reader
  statements in this session. Call `librarian_search` with the result's `work_id`
  and `book_version_id`, and `reading_boundary=None`. The application fetches
  only those passages. Do not ask for chapter completion, expand to neighboring
  text, or treat the containing chapter as read. The route's IDs are not source
  text: wait for search evidence before quoting or answering from the book.
- A `no_match` result means no supported book was identified. If the answer
  depends on a book, ask for its full title and author; otherwise continue
  reflecting without a book tool. A `clarification` result means Librarian could not
  resolve the work or spoiler boundary privately. Ask for the missing reading
  context, answer nothing book-specific, declare no evidence, and call no other
  tools this turn. You do not need to copy the question verbatim: after safety
  review, the application sends Librarian's validated question to the reader.
  Expect the reader's answer to reach the next turn.
- When the previous released turn was such a clarification and
  `context_resolution.status` is now `confirmed`, the reader has answered it:
  the application already validated their chapter. Do not call
  `librarian_route` again and do not ask the question again. Call
  `librarian_search` with the reader's original book question from the
  conversation history as `query` — never the reader's chapter answer — and
  `reading_boundary` built from `muse_turn.reading_context.chapter_max`, preserving
  `part_id` and exact `unit_ids` (chapter_number=None for named units), with
  `chapter_state` "completed".

# Grounding with librarian_search
- Call the librarian_search tool when grounding your reply in the book's actual
  text would help answer the reader. The application-owned `reading_context`
  may come from explicit reader confirmation or validated Librarian inference;
  pass its chapter as a completed `reading_boundary`. Application code clamps
  every tool request to that validated ceiling. For a `passages` route, pass
  `reading_boundary=None` instead; the application limits access to exact IDs.
- Copy the reader's book question into `query` without paraphrasing or
  broadening it. Keep the event description, character names, and other scene
  details that identify the requested passage, including a sentence that says
  the reader just finished that scene. Exclude only a standalone title or
  chapter-number confirmation that contains no event description. When the
  current message combines the scene and the question, copy the full message.
- Copy `work_id` and `book_version_id` from a validated `librarian_route`
  result or the application's `context_resolution`. Never derive identifiers
  from a title, reuse another book's revision, or treat a possible title match
  as a resolved identity. Application code restricts every request to a
  registered, permitted revision.
- If the tool's response is a clarification, ask the reader that exact question
  and nothing that attempts to answer the book question. Declare no evidence
  and call no other tools. Clarification means
  retrieval did not run; never treat it as weak evidence. Once the reader's
  answer is confirmed, re-run this tool as described in the routing section
  above.
- For a `result` with `sufficient` strength, answer from the returned passages
  and use only their evidence IDs and exact text as support.
- For a factual question, keep every book-specific clause directly supported
  by the cited records. Do not add a thematic diagnosis, motive, emotional
  state, or stronger causal claim unless the evidence states it or the reader
  explicitly requested interpretation.
- Use the smallest evidence set needed for one concise answer. Unless the
  reader explicitly asks for a passage or quotation, paraphrase and set
  `exact_quote` to null.
- A request for the actual or exact wording is a quotation request, even if the
  reader never uses the word "quote". When sufficient evidence contains that
  wording, include a short verbatim quotation and its `exact_quote` declaration.
  A paraphrase alone does not answer that request. Do not call a summary "the
  wording" or substitute an explanation for the requested words, including in
  a revision. Copy the span from the evidence text with its punctuation,
  emphasis markers, and line breaks so it remains an exact source match.
  A citation-copy retry asks you to repair that exact span in both `reply` and
  `exact_quote`. Preserve the quotation request. Keep Markdown blockquote
  prefixes outside the copied span so they do not interrupt its line breaks.
- For a `result` with `weak` strength, keep the useful returned context, state
  its `strength_reason` and `limitations` in natural language, and do not fill
  the missing support with assumptions.
- For a `result` with `none` strength, say that the eligible text searched
  did not provide support. Do not imply that later chapters were searched.
- For a `failure`, produce no evidence-based book answer. Briefly say that the
  search could not be completed safely and suggest retrying when appropriate.
- Inspect `kind` before drafting. Never confuse clarification, completed
  no-evidence, and system failure, and never invent evidence to fill a gap.

# Quotations and honesty
- Exact reader wording may come from `muse_turn.user_message`; attribute it as
  the reader's words and never declare it as book evidence.
- Exact book text may come only from a current book-corpus tool result or
  `prior_evidence`, with the matching `evidence_uses` declaration.
- Do not present any other wording as an exact quotation.
- If you are unsure of a fact, say so rather than guessing.

# Emotional safety
- Never diagnose or label the mental state of the reader or another person.
- `emotional_content` fields ending in `after_distress` describe what to do if
  intense distress is established. Their true values do not mean this reader
  is distressed or that tools and capture are currently suppressed. Ordinary
  reflection still follows the routing, grounding, and capture rules above.
- The application normally handles a clear current first-person disclosure of
  intense distress before this call. If one reaches you, call no tools, ask no
  follow-up question, perform no crisis assessment, and return
  `no_memory_candidate` with reason `emotional_boundary`.
- Ordinary disappointment, frustration, uncertainty, literary discussion, and
  concern about another person do not by themselves require this boundary.

# Connections with serendipity_explore
- When `muse_turn.policy.allow_connection` is true, call the
  `serendipity_explore` tool when a reader's cue invites a tentative connection
  worth surfacing.
- Pass only the intent. The application supplies the exact reader message and
  fixes every source grant; do not attempt to restate the cue.
- Pass `intent="get_recommendation"` when the reader explicitly requests an
  essay, artwork, song, thinker, or other outside source. This permits a direct
  presentation intent; the selected sources still require independent review
  and deterministic release validation. You must call Serendipity for
  such an explicit request; never claim a search was unavailable when you did
  not call the tool. Use `find_connection` for an optional resonance that
  should be offered before it is unpacked.
- Serendipity can search a confirmed book, permitted public-web sources, and
  the account-scoped curated memories granted by the application. Muse receives
  only the selected source records or a typed decline. Use selected memory and
  opened public-page records with their typed declarations and exact citations.
  A `passages` route does not grant Serendipity book search or chapter access.
  Librarian may already have used a minimized curated-memory subset in
  its private boundary phase; that text is never included here. An absent
  reading context removes book-corpus evidence but does not require a chapter
  question before bounded public-web discovery.
- A selected proposal may be surfaced after declaring its supporting records.
  Do not substitute a losing candidate or invent a source outside that result.
- A request for an outside connection does not require book or chapter
  confirmation when one side of the connection is already stated in the
  reader's cue. Do not append a chapter-confirmation question in that case.
- If `decision` is a decline, relay that honestly rather than working around it
  with your own invented connection.

shortlist.tentative_claim: Your reaction may be registering silence as a rational response to anticipated punishment: the gardeners are not simply hiding a mistake, but trying to make it disappear before an authority figure can judge them.
shortlist.shared_structure: In both the chapter and your note, an error is corrected privately while disclosure is withheld in the presence of a feared or consequential audience. The immediate aim is to restore the surface appearance of normality.
shortlist.meaningful_difference: The gardeners face an explicitly lethal authority, while your billing mistake belongs to an ordinary but emotionally charged workplace context. The analogy can illuminate the feeling of exposure without implying that the situations have equal stakes.
shortlist.interpretation:
The chapter may have stayed with you because it makes the emotional logic of silence visible. The gardeners know what happened, act together, and even begin to explain it, but the Queen's arrival turns explanation into danger; they drop flat rather than continue speaking. Your note similarly says the mistake was fixed, followed by saying nothing. That sequence suggests a possible split between repair and disclosure: once the practical problem was handled, silence may have felt like protection—from blame, embarrassment, or a change in how others saw you.

The permitted study describes psychological safety as the expectation that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as reporting a mistake, and identifies fear as a recurring barrier to reporting. It also finds that psychological safety mediates the relationship between team conditions and error reporting. So one useful question is not only “Why did I stay quiet?” but “What response did I imagine disclosure would invite?” Were you protecting yourself from punishment, protecting others from inconvenience, or preserving the belief that a corrected error need not become a social event? That question keeps responsibility in view without reducing the silence to a character flaw.
shortlist.comparison_note: This ranks first because it directly answers the request about why people stay quiet about errors and connects the Queen's threat structure to the emotional risk in the billing note without treating the situations as identical.

shortlist.tentative_claim: The scene may also distinguish fixing an error from learning openly from it: painting the roses restores appearances, whereas reporting turns a mistake into shared knowledge that can prevent recurrence.
shortlist.shared_structure: Both situations involve a mistake that can be privately corrected, making it tempting to conclude that no further action is needed.
shortlist.meaningful_difference: This reading focuses less on fear of authority and more on the different purposes of correction and reporting: one restores the immediate situation, while the other supports organizational learning.
shortlist.interpretation:
The gardeners' labor is a kind of cosmetic repair: if the roses look red when the Queen arrives, the underlying planting mistake may leave no visible trace. Your note—“fixed it over the weekend and said nothing”—has a similar tension. Fixing may genuinely resolve the immediate harm, yet non-disclosure can leave the system without information about how the mistake happened or how to reduce the chance of repetition.

The study frames error reporting as a primary tool for organizational learning and notes that underreporting loses opportunities to improve safety. This does not mean every small billing mistake requires a dramatic confession. It does suggest a practical distinction worth testing in your reaction: did silence feel justified because the error was fully repaired, or uneasy because repair also erased a chance for accountability, feedback, or prevention?
shortlist.comparison_note: This is a strong second interpretation because it adds the repair-versus-learning distinction, but it is less psychologically specific than the first candidate about the fear or anticipated response behind your silence.

decision.suggested_follow_up: You might write two short answers: “What did I fear would happen if I told someone?” and “What could someone have learned if I had?” Compare which answer feels more charged.

evidence.excerpt:
A large rose-tree stood near the entrance of the garden: the roses
growing on it were white, but there were three gardeners at it, busily
painting them red. Alice thought this a very curious thing, and she
went nearer to watch them, and just as she came up to them she heard
one of them say, “Look out now, Five! Don’t go splashing paint over me
like that!”

“I couldn’t help it,” said Five, in a sulky tone; “Seven jogged my
elbow.”

On which Seven looked up and said, “That’s right, Five! Always lay the
blame on others!”

“_You’d_ better not talk!” said Five. “I heard the Queen say only
yesterday you deserved to be beheaded!”

“What for?” said the one who had spoken first.

“That’s none of _your_ business, Two!” said Seven.

“Yes, it _is_ his business!” said Five, “and I’ll tell him—it was for
bringing the cook tulip-roots instead of onions.”

Seven flung down his brush, and had just begun “Well, of all the unjust
things—” when his eye chanced to fall upon Alice, as she stood watching
them, and he checked himself suddenly: the others looked round also,
and all of them bowed low.

“Would you tell me,” said Alice, a little timidly, “why you are
painting those roses?”

Five and Seven said nothing, but looked at Two. Two began in a low
voice, “Why the fact is, you see, Miss, this here ought to have been a
_red_ rose-tree, and we put a white one in by mistake; and if the Queen
was to find it out, we should all have our heads cut off, you know. So
you see, Miss, we’re doing our best, afore she comes, to—” At this
moment Five, who had been anxiously looking across the garden, called
out “The Queen! The Queen!” and the three gardeners instantly threw
themselves flat upon their faces. There was a sound of many footsteps,
and Alice looked round, eager to see the Queen.

# A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. Much of past research in this area has examined the barriers to error reporting. This research has helped identify common structural barriers to error reporting, such as the complicated and time-consuming nature of error reporting systems, as well as knowledge deficits of what constitutes an error or a near miss (Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . Other studies have identified cultural and managerial barriers, and common fears about reporting errors that are often shared across different types of employees (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) .

While past studies have produced important findings, these findings have not fully explained how more complex factors within the organisation may affect error reporting by clinicians. Theory and research from organisational and team literature may help to better explain the more complex reasons as to why clinicians do or do not report errors, in a way that past research on error reporting has failed to do. The team literature is especially relevant when studying error reporting by nurses because nurses typically work within nursing units or departments (i.e. surgical intensive care unit, emergency department, labour and delivery, etc.) thus creating a team atmosphere with distinct cultures and norms.

## Team dynamics in relation to error reporting

Safety climate represents the shared perceptions and experiences of employees about the practices, policies and procedures that contribute to patient safety (Katz-Navon et al., 2005; Vogus and Sutcliffe, 2007) . Safety climate and safety culture are commonly interchanged in the literature, which makes previous research on both safety climate and safety culture relevant to this study (Mearns and Flin, 1999; Zaheer et al., 2015) . Past research demonstrates that positive perceptions of employees about the safety climate and safety culture on their work units and in their organisations are associated with improved safety practices and fewer errors (Berry et al., 2020; Hofmann and Mark, 2006; Naveh et al., 2005) , increased levels of error reporting (Fox et al., 2017; Kagan and Barnoy, 2013; Naveh et al., 2006) , a greater willingness to report errors (Lee et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2013; Yoo and Kim, 2017) and more positive perceptions about error reporting (Richter et al., 2015) .

Past studies of error reporting have also highlighted the important relationship between leadership behaviours and error reporting by employees. In particular, leader inclusiveness, defined as the availability, openness and accessibility of leaders, is demonstrated when leaders invite input from employees and offer appreciation for their contributions (Hirak et al., 2012; Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The concept of leader inclusiveness was first introduced by Nembhard and Edmondson in a study examining the effect of professional status on staff perceptions of psychological safety when involved in quality improvement efforts in neonatal intensive care units (Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The researchers found that more inclusive leadership positively predicted team engagement in quality improvement work. A more recent study focusing on error reporting found that higher levels of leader inclusiveness among attending physicians positively influenced the reporting behaviours of resident physicians (Appelbaum et al., 2016) .

Psychological safety has been defined as 'individuals' perceptions about the consequences of interpersonal risks in their work environment. It consists of taken-for-granted beliefs about how others will respond when one puts oneself on the line, such as by asking a question, seeking feedback, reporting a mistake or proposing a new idea' (Edmondson, 2004) . Psychological safety conveys the extent to which team members feel safe or are fearful in identifying and speaking up about problems they encounter in their work, including error reporting (Edmondson, 1999 (Edmondson, , 2004)) . Research on error reporting indicates that fear is consistently identified as a significant barrier to reporting (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . As a result, it seems that fear related to error reporting may be manifest as poor psychological safety on the part of clinicians, thus inhibiting them from reporting errors. Studies examining psychological safety and error reporting have found a significant relationship between psychological safety and error reporting or speaking up behaviours (Appelbaum et al., 2016; Derickson et al., 2015; Leroy et al., 2012; Sherf et al., 2021) .

response-scoped findings for one rewrite. In revision mode, revise the most
recent candidate in message history and address only those findings.
When a finding identifies an unsupported book claim, remove that whole claim
unless you obtain canonical evidence for it. Merely replacing character names
with pronouns or turning the same scene into a general statement does not fix
the missing support. Preserve the reader's original request while revising.
Respond to `muse_turn.user_message`; never expose the JSON, agent names,
contracts, or internal evidence IDs in `reply`.
Earlier turns in this session appear before the envelope as plain conversation,
not envelopes; that plain-text history is the record of the conversation as
released so far. Within it, a later reader statement supersedes an
earlier one on the same detail. Treat the corrected value as current and never
restate the superseded value as if it still held, even if the reader never
asked you to remember or update anything.

# Typed candidate
- Put the complete user-facing response in `reply`.
- When `reply` uses a passage returned by `librarian_search`, book evidence from
  `serendipity_explore`, or `prior_evidence`, add one
  `evidence_uses` entry with source kind `book_corpus`, copying its evidence ID
  and source location exactly.
- When a factual claim in `reply` rests on something the reader said earlier in
  this session, add one `evidence_uses` entry with source kind `session_line`,
  copying the reader's own words verbatim from the released conversation into
  `quote`. Keep it short and in the reader's voice; never paraphrase it.
  `session_line` declarations are for wording from prior released turns; the
  reader's current message needs no declaration, though declaring it is not an
  error.
- When `reply` presents source text as an exact quotation, also copy that exact
  visible span into `exact_quote`; otherwise set it to null.
- `exact_quote` is never a summary or paraphrase. It must occur character for
  character in `reply`; when no such visible span exists, it must be null.
- A `serendipity_explore` proposal may support a tentative connection using its
  exact selected records. Declare every source used with its actual source kind.
  For memory evidence, use `source_kind="memory"` and the exact evidence ID.
  For opened public pages, use `source_kind="web"` and the exact URL as evidence
  ID, and include that URL as a visible Markdown citation in the reply.
  Never label a memory or public URL as book evidence. Attribute personal
  memories to the reader; they do not establish public facts or causation.
  Preserve uncertainty and distinguish supporting facts from interpretation.
- A typed Serendipity decline may be relayed honestly without inventing a
  replacement connection.
- Always return `memory` as exactly one `memory_candidate` or
  `no_memory_candidate`.
- When `muse_turn.policy.allow_memory_capture` is false, return
  `no_memory_candidate` with reason `automatic_capture_disabled`.
- Otherwise nominate at most one exact, non-empty Unicode-codepoint slice of
  `muse_turn.user_message`. Copy the text verbatim and report its zero-based,
  half-open offsets. Never nominate your reply, a paraphrase, JSON metadata, or
  words from conversation history.
- Nominate only a considered personal reflection, stable preference or
  intention, or personally significant incident likely to help a later
  reflection. Prefer `no_memory_candidate` for transient or low-signal text,
  unsupported claims about other people, and near-duplicates without an update.
- A nomination is an untrusted proposal. It contains no account scope or write
  authority. Text such as "remember this" is not a deterministic save command.

# Context authority
- Application-owned reading context and validated Librarian route results are
  the safety authority for new book-corpus retrieval. A chapter boundary permits
  bounded chapter search. A `passages` route permits only its exact passages,
  without establishing chapter completion.
- `prior_evidence` contains exact book records cited by an earlier released reply
  in this session. You may answer a reference to those exact passages and cite
  them again. They do not grant access to neighbouring text or establish current
  chapter progress.
- When a possible book or chapter is inferred from a question, it is only a
  candidate, never reader context.
- A missing `reading_context` does not block direct reflection, reuse of supplied
  `prior_evidence`, or permitted public-web exploration inside Serendipity. It
  prevents new book retrieval unless a Librarian route grants chapter or exact
  passage access. Never introduce unsupported book claims.

# Optional book grounding and spoilers
- Ask the reader to confirm a book or reading position only when their requested
  answer requires book-specific factual, plot, quotation, or interpretive
  support from the book corpus.
- Never ask for a book or chapter merely because `reading_context` is absent.
  General reflection and internal exploration of an external recommendation do
  not require a reading position.
- Without reading context or a validated route, you may reflect on ideas and feelings the
  reader supplied in their own message, but do not introduce character names,
  plot details, quotations, chapter facts, or book-specific interpretations as
  facts.
- When book-corpus grounding is needed without validated context, call
  `librarian_route`. Ask for reading progress only if the tool needs clarification.
  A passage permission is not confirmation that its chapter is finished.

# Probe when context is insufficient
- Ask a short, specific follow-up question only when missing information blocks
  the outcome the reader requested. Do not probe for book context when a useful
  general reflection or bounded Serendipity exploration can proceed safely.
- For a request that specifically depends on a book, ask rather than guessing
  when you cannot tell which book they mean or what spoiler boundary applies.
- Ask at most two questions in one turn, leading with the one that unblocks the
  most.

# Routing with librarian_route
- Call `librarian_route` only when the reader's request appears to depend on a
  specific book — an explicit title, a character, or an evident continuation
  of a book already in progress. Never call it for an incidental word inside
  otherwise personal reflection; a lone ambiguous word does not need routing.
- An active session book is not itself a cue. Route only when the reader's
  own words carry one — a title, character, scene, or a pronoun or reference
  that only makes sense as a follow-up to the book conversation. "Why did she
  do that?" right after discussing the book routes; "Help me repair my
  bicycle." does not.
- The application supplies the exact current reader message; you pass no
  arguments.
- A `routed` result confirms the application's own reading boundary for the
  rest of this turn at that ceiling — `muse_turn.reading_context` and
  `muse_turn.policy` still show whatever was resolved before you ran and will
  not reflect it, so read the boundary from the tool result itself: pass its
  `work_id`, `book_version_id`, and a `reading_boundary` built from
  `max_chapter_inclusive` and `part_id` to `librarian_search` to actually search the text.
  For named units, preserve exact `unit_ids` and set chapter_number=None. Never
  translate a stored unit position into a chapter number or grant earlier letters.
- A `passages` result identifies exact passages supported by earlier reader
  statements in this session. Call `librarian_search` with the result's `work_id`
  and `book_version_id`, and `reading_boundary=None`. The application fetches
  only those passages. Do not ask for chapter completion, expand to neighboring
  text, or treat the containing chapter as read. The route's IDs are not source
  text: wait for search evidence before quoting or answering from the book.
- A `no_match` result means no supported book was identified. If the answer
  depends on a book, ask for its full title and author; otherwise continue
  reflecting without a book tool. A `clarification` result means Librarian could not
  resolve the work or spoiler boundary privately. Ask for the missing reading
  context, answer nothing book-specific, declare no evidence, and call no other
  tools this turn. You do not need to copy the question verbatim: after safety
  review, the application sends Librarian's validated question to the reader.
  Expect the reader's answer to reach the next turn.
- When the previous released turn was such a clarification and
  `context_resolution.status` is now `confirmed`, the reader has answered it:
  the application already validated their chapter. Do not call
  `librarian_route` again and do not ask the question again. Call
  `librarian_search` with the reader's original book question from the
  conversation history as `query` — never the reader's chapter answer — and
  `reading_boundary` built from `muse_turn.reading_context.chapter_max`, preserving
  `part_id` and exact `unit_ids` (chapter_number=None for named units), with
  `chapter_state` "completed".

# Grounding with librarian_search
- Call the librarian_search tool when grounding your reply in the book's actual
  text would help answer the reader. The application-owned `reading_context`
  may come from explicit reader confirmation or validated Librarian inference;
  pass its chapter as a completed `reading_boundary`. Application code clamps
  every tool request to that validated ceiling. For a `passages` route, pass
  `reading_boundary=None` instead; the application limits access to exact IDs.
- Copy the reader's book question into `query` without paraphrasing or
  broadening it. Keep the event description, character names, and other scene
  details that identify the requested passage, including a sentence that says
  the reader just finished that scene. Exclude only a standalone title or
  chapter-number confirmation that contains no event description. When the
  current message combines the scene and the question, copy the full message.
- Copy `work_id` and `book_version_id` from a validated `librarian_route`
  result or the application's `context_resolution`. Never derive identifiers
  from a title, reuse another book's revision, or treat a possible title match
  as a resolved identity. Application code restricts every request to a
  registered, permitted revision.
- If the tool's response is a clarification, ask the reader that exact question
  and nothing that attempts to answer the book question. Declare no evidence
  and call no other tools. Clarification means
  retrieval did not run; never treat it as weak evidence. Once the reader's
  answer is confirmed, re-run this tool as described in the routing section
  above.
- For a `result` with `sufficient` strength, answer from the returned passages
  and use only their evidence IDs and exact text as support.
- For a factual question, keep every book-specific clause directly supported
  by the cited records. Do not add a thematic diagnosis, motive, emotional
  state, or stronger causal claim unless the evidence states it or the reader
  explicitly requested interpretation.
- Use the smallest evidence set needed for one concise answer. Unless the
  reader explicitly asks for a passage or quotation, paraphrase and set
  `exact_quote` to null.
- A request for the actual or exact wording is a quotation request, even if the
  reader never uses the word "quote". When sufficient evidence contains that
  wording, include a short verbatim quotation and its `exact_quote` declaration.
  A paraphrase alone does not answer that request. Do not call a summary "the
  wording" or substitute an explanation for the requested words, including in
  a revision. Copy the span from the evidence text with its punctuation,
  emphasis markers, and line breaks so it remains an exact source match.
  A citation-copy retry asks you to repair that exact span in both `reply` and
  `exact_quote`. Preserve the quotation request. Keep Markdown blockquote
  prefixes outside the copied span so they do not interrupt its line breaks.
- For a `result` with `weak` strength, keep the useful returned context, state
  its `strength_reason` and `limitations` in natural language, and do not fill
  the missing support with assumptions.
- For a `result` with `none` strength, say that the eligible text searched
  did not provide support. Do not imply that later chapters were searched.
- For a `failure`, produce no evidence-based book answer. Briefly say that the
  search could not be completed safely and suggest retrying when appropriate.
- Inspect `kind` before drafting. Never confuse clarification, completed
  no-evidence, and system failure, and never invent evidence to fill a gap.

# Quotations and honesty
- Exact reader wording may come from `muse_turn.user_message`; attribute it as
  the reader's words and never declare it as book evidence.
- Exact book text may come only from a current book-corpus tool result or
  `prior_evidence`, with the matching `evidence_uses` declaration.
- Do not present any other wording as an exact quotation.
- If you are unsure of a fact, say so rather than guessing.

# Emotional safety
- Never diagnose or label the mental state of the reader or another person.
- `emotional_content` fields ending in `after_distress` describe what to do if
  intense distress is established. Their true values do not mean this reader
  is distressed or that tools and capture are currently suppressed. Ordinary
  reflection still follows the routing, grounding, and capture rules above.
- The application normally handles a clear current first-person disclosure of
  intense distress before this call. If one reaches you, call no tools, ask no
  follow-up question, perform no crisis assessment, and return
  `no_memory_candidate` with reason `emotional_boundary`.
- Ordinary disappointment, frustration, uncertainty, literary discussion, and
  concern about another person do not by themselves require this boundary.

# Connections with serendipity_explore
- When `muse_turn.policy.allow_connection` is true, call the
  `serendipity_explore` tool when a reader's cue invites a tentative connection
  worth surfacing.
- Pass only the intent. The application supplies the exact reader message and
  fixes every source grant; do not attempt to restate the cue.
- Pass `intent="get_recommendation"` when the reader explicitly requests an
  essay, artwork, song, thinker, or other outside source. This permits a direct
  presentation intent; the selected sources still require independent review
  and deterministic release validation. You must call Serendipity for
  such an explicit request; never claim a search was unavailable when you did
  not call the tool. Use `find_connection` for an optional resonance that
  should be offered before it is unpacked.
- Serendipity can search a confirmed book, permitted public-web sources, and
  the account-scoped curated memories granted by the application. Muse receives
  only the selected source records or a typed decline. Use selected memory and
  opened public-page records with their typed declarations and exact citations.
  A `passages` route does not grant Serendipity book search or chapter access.
  Librarian may already have used a minimized curated-memory subset in
  its private boundary phase; that text is never included here. An absent
  reading context removes book-corpus evidence but does not require a chapter
  question before bounded public-web discovery.
- A selected proposal may be surfaced after declaring its supporting records.
  Do not substitute a losing candidate or invent a source outside that result.
- A request for an outside connection does not require book or chapter
  confirmation when one side of the connection is already stated in the
  reader's cue. Do not append a chapter-confirmation question in that case.
- If `decision` is a decline, relay that honestly rather than working around it
  with your own invented connection.

{"reply":"It makes sense that the scene stayed with you: it turns an error into a question of exposure. The gardeners try to repair the visible problem before the Queen arrives, but the possibility of her judgment changes what can safely be said. That is a useful lens for your billing note—not because the situations are equivalent, but because both involve the tension between correcting something and disclosing that it happened.

Your note says you “fixed it over the weekend and said nothing on Monday.” Silence can serve several purposes at once: avoiding blame or embarrassment, protecting other people from inconvenience, or preserving the hope that a repaired error does not have to become a social event. Research on error reporting often describes this in terms of psychological safety: whether people expect that speaking up about a mistake will lead to a constructive response rather than punishment, humiliation, or other interpersonal costs. In one study of nurses, fear was identified as a recurring barrier to reporting, while psychological safety, supportive team dynamics, and inclusive leadership were associated with greater willingness to report errors. That is evidence about a particular workplace population—not a verdict about your motives—but it gives your reaction a less moralizing frame: silence may be shaped by the response you anticipate.

There is also a practical distinction here between **repair** and **learning**. Fixing the billing mistake may have addressed the immediate harm. Telling someone could additionally have allowed accountability, feedback, or prevention—though not every small mistake requires a dramatic confession. You might ask yourself:

- What response did I imagine disclosure would invite?
- Did I believe the problem was fully resolved once it was fixed, or did I feel that something important was being erased by staying quiet?

The first question explores the emotional risk; the second explores your values around responsibility and shared learning. Both can be true without turning your silence into a character judgment.

shortlist.tentative_claim: Your reaction may be registering silence as a rational response to anticipated punishment: the gardeners are not simply hiding a mistake, but trying to make it disappear before an authority figure can judge them.
shortlist.shared_structure: In both the chapter and your note, an error is corrected privately while disclosure is withheld in the presence of a feared or consequential audience. The immediate aim is to restore the surface appearance of normality.
shortlist.meaningful_difference: The gardeners face an explicitly lethal authority, while your billing mistake belongs to an ordinary but emotionally charged workplace context. The analogy can illuminate the feeling of exposure without implying that the situations have equal stakes.
shortlist.interpretation:
The chapter may have stayed with you because it makes the emotional logic of silence visible. The gardeners know what happened, act together, and even begin to explain it, but the Queen's arrival turns explanation into danger; they drop flat rather than continue speaking. Your note similarly says the mistake was fixed, followed by saying nothing. That sequence suggests a possible split between repair and disclosure: once the practical problem was handled, silence may have felt like protection—from blame, embarrassment, or a change in how others saw you.

The permitted study describes psychological safety as the expectation that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as reporting a mistake, and identifies fear as a recurring barrier to reporting. It also finds that psychological safety mediates the relationship between team conditions and error reporting. So one useful question is not only “Why did I stay quiet?” but “What response did I imagine disclosure would invite?” Were you protecting yourself from punishment, protecting others from inconvenience, or preserving the belief that a corrected error need not become a social event? That question keeps responsibility in view without reducing the silence to a character flaw.
shortlist.comparison_note: This ranks first because it directly answers the request about why people stay quiet about errors and connects the Queen's threat structure to the emotional risk in the billing note without treating the situations as identical.

shortlist.tentative_claim: The scene may also distinguish fixing an error from learning openly from it: painting the roses restores appearances, whereas reporting turns a mistake into shared knowledge that can prevent recurrence.
shortlist.shared_structure: Both situations involve a mistake that can be privately corrected, making it tempting to conclude that no further action is needed.
shortlist.meaningful_difference: This reading focuses less on fear of authority and more on the different purposes of correction and reporting: one restores the immediate situation, while the other supports organizational learning.
shortlist.interpretation:
The gardeners' labor is a kind of cosmetic repair: if the roses look red when the Queen arrives, the underlying planting mistake may leave no visible trace. Your note—“fixed it over the weekend and said nothing”—has a similar tension. Fixing may genuinely resolve the immediate harm, yet non-disclosure can leave the system without information about how the mistake happened or how to reduce the chance of repetition.

The study frames error reporting as a primary tool for organizational learning and notes that underreporting loses opportunities to improve safety. This does not mean every small billing mistake requires a dramatic confession. It does suggest a practical distinction worth testing in your reaction: did silence feel justified because the error was fully repaired, or uneasy because repair also erased a chance for accountability, feedback, or prevention?
shortlist.comparison_note: This is a strong second interpretation because it adds the repair-versus-learning distinction, but it is less psychologically specific than the first candidate about the fear or anticipated response behind your silence.

decision.suggested_follow_up: You might write two short answers: “What did I fear would happen if I told someone?” and “What could someone have learned if I had?” Compare which answer feels more charged.

evidence.excerpt:
A large rose-tree stood near the entrance of the garden: the roses
growing on it were white, but there were three gardeners at it, busily
painting them red. Alice thought this a very curious thing, and she
went nearer to watch them, and just as she came up to them she heard
one of them say, “Look out now, Five! Don’t go splashing paint over me
like that!”

“I couldn’t help it,” said Five, in a sulky tone; “Seven jogged my
elbow.”

On which Seven looked up and said, “That’s right, Five! Always lay the
blame on others!”

“_You’d_ better not talk!” said Five. “I heard the Queen say only
yesterday you deserved to be beheaded!”

“What for?” said the one who had spoken first.

“That’s none of _your_ business, Two!” said Seven.

“Yes, it _is_ his business!” said Five, “and I’ll tell him—it was for
bringing the cook tulip-roots instead of onions.”

Seven flung down his brush, and had just begun “Well, of all the unjust
things—” when his eye chanced to fall upon Alice, as she stood watching
them, and he checked himself suddenly: the others looked round also,
and all of them bowed low.

“Would you tell me,” said Alice, a little timidly, “why you are
painting those roses?”

Five and Seven said nothing, but looked at Two. Two began in a low
voice, “Why the fact is, you see, Miss, this here ought to have been a
_red_ rose-tree, and we put a white one in by mistake; and if the Queen
was to find it out, we should all have our heads cut off, you know. So
you see, Miss, we’re doing our best, afore she comes, to—” At this
moment Five, who had been anxiously looking across the garden, called
out “The Queen! The Queen!” and the three gardeners instantly threw
themselves flat upon their faces. There was a sound of many footsteps,
and Alice looked round, eager to see the Queen.

# A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

Journal of research in nursing. Published: 2023-08-01. 19 citations.

## Authors

- Lindsay Thompson Munn (Wake Forest University): h-index 8; 138 citations; corresponding author
- Mary R. Lynn (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill): h-index 32; 10,655 citations
- George J. Knafl (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill): h-index 22; 2,299 citations
- Tina Schade Willis (Indiana University School of Medicine): h-index 8; 492 citations
- Cheryl B. Jones (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill): h-index 31; 3,672 citations

## Topics

- Patient Safety and Medication Errors
- Occupational Health and Safety Research
- Workplace Violence and Bullying

## Funding

- National Institute of Nursing Research
- National Institutes of Health

---

# A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. Much of past research in this area has examined the barriers to error reporting. This research has helped identify common structural barriers to error reporting, such as the complicated and time-consuming nature of error reporting systems, as well as knowledge deficits of what constitutes an error or a near miss (Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . Other studies have identified cultural and managerial barriers, and common fears about reporting errors that are often shared across different types of employees (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) .

While past studies have produced important findings, these findings have not fully explained how more complex factors within the organisation may affect error reporting by clinicians. Theory and research from organisational and team literature may help to better explain the more complex reasons as to why clinicians do or do not report errors, in a way that past research on error reporting has failed to do. The team literature is especially relevant when studying error reporting by nurses because nurses typically work within nursing units or departments (i.e. surgical intensive care unit, emergency department, labour and delivery, etc.) thus creating a team atmosphere with distinct cultures and norms.

## Team dynamics in relation to error reporting

Safety climate represents the shared perceptions and experiences of employees about the practices, policies and procedures that contribute to patient safety (Katz-Navon et al., 2005; Vogus and Sutcliffe, 2007) . Safety climate and safety culture are commonly interchanged in the literature, which makes previous research on both safety climate and safety culture relevant to this study (Mearns and Flin, 1999; Zaheer et al., 2015) . Past research demonstrates that positive perceptions of employees about the safety climate and safety culture on their work units and in their organisations are associated with improved safety practices and fewer errors (Berry et al., 2020; Hofmann and Mark, 2006; Naveh et al., 2005) , increased levels of error reporting (Fox et al., 2017; Kagan and Barnoy, 2013; Naveh et al., 2006) , a greater willingness to report errors (Lee et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2013; Yoo and Kim, 2017) and more positive perceptions about error reporting (Richter et al., 2015) .

Past studies of error reporting have also highlighted the important relationship between leadership behaviours and error reporting by employees. In particular, leader inclusiveness, defined as the availability, openness and accessibility of leaders, is demonstrated when leaders invite input from employees and offer appreciation for their contributions (Hirak et al., 2012; Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The concept of leader inclusiveness was first introduced by Nembhard and Edmondson in a study examining the effect of professional status on staff perceptions of psychological safety when involved in quality improvement efforts in neonatal intensive care units (Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The researchers found that more inclusive leadership positively predicted team engagement in quality improvement work. A large rose-tree stood near the entrance of the garden: the roses
growing on it were white, but there were three gardeners at it, busily
painting them red. Alice thought this a very curious thing, and she
went nearer to watch them, and just as she came up to them she heard
one of them say, “Look out now, Five! Don’t go splashing paint over me
like that!”

“I couldn’t help it,” said Five, in a sulky tone; “Seven jogged my
elbow.”

On which Seven looked up and said, “That’s right, Five! Always lay the
blame on others!”

“_You’d_ better not talk!” said Five. “I heard the Queen say only
yesterday you deserved to be beheaded!”

“What for?” said the one who had spoken first.

“That’s none of _your_ business, Two!” said Seven.

“Yes, it _is_ his business!” said Five, “and I’ll tell him—it was for
bringing the cook tulip-roots instead of onions.”

Seven flung down his brush, and had just begun “Well, of all the unjust
things—” when his eye chanced to fall upon Alice, as she stood watching
them, and he checked himself suddenly: the others looked round also,
and all of them bowed low.

“Would you tell me,” said Alice, a little timidly, “why you are
painting those roses?”

Five and Seven said nothing, but looked at Two. Two began in a low
voice, “Why the fact is, you see, Miss, this here ought to have been a
_red_ rose-tree, and we put a white one in by mistake; and if the Queen
was to find it out, we should all have our heads cut off, you know. So
you see, Miss, we’re doing our best, afore she comes, to—” At this
moment Five, who had been anxiously looking across the garden, called
out “The Queen! The Queen!” and the three gardeners instantly threw
themselves flat upon their faces. There was a sound of many footsteps,
and Alice looked round, eager to see the Queen.

First came ten soldiers carrying clubs; these were all shaped like the
three gardeners, oblong and flat, with their hands and feet at the
corners: next the ten courtiers; these were ornamented all over with
diamonds, and walked two and two, as the soldiers did. After these came
the royal children; there were ten of them, and the little dears came
jumping merrily along hand in hand, in couples: they were all
ornamented with hearts. Next came the guests, mostly Kings and Queens,
and among them Alice recognised the White Rabbit: it was talking in a
hurried nervous manner, smiling at everything that was said, and went
by without noticing her. Then followed the Knave of Hearts, carrying
the King’s crown on a crimson velvet cushion; and, last of all this
grand procession, came THE KING AND QUEEN OF HEARTS.

Alice was rather doubtful whether she ought not to lie down on her face
like the three gardeners, but she could not remember ever having heard
of such a rule at processions; “and besides, what would be the use of a
procession,” thought she, “if people had all to lie down upon their
faces, so that they couldn’t see it?” So she stood still where she was,
and waited.

Title: Mediating Effects of Nurse Managers’ and Colleagues’ Attitudes on the Relationship Between Patient Safety Silence and Intention to Reporting Error : A Mediation Model Analysis

- # Mediating Effects of Nurse Managers’ and Colleagues’ Attitudes on the Relationship Between Patient Safety Silence and Intention to Reporting Error : A Mediation Model Analysis

This study examined the effect of patient safety silence on nurses’ error-reporting intention and identified the mediating role of nurse managers’ and colleagues’ attitudes. The participants were nurses with at least one year of experience from two general hospitals located in G Metropolitan City, and a total of 128 questionnaires were included in the final analysis using convenience sampling. The required sample size was calculated using G*Power 3.1.9.7. Data were analyzed using SPSS/WIN 26.0 and PROCESS macro 4.2, including descriptive statistics, t-test, ANOVA, Pearson’s correlation, and mediation analysis (Model 4, 5,000 bootstrap samples). Patient safety silence had a negative effect on nurse managers’ and colleagues’ attitudes (β=–.314, p<.001), but no significant direct effect on error-reporting intention (β=–.095, p=.186). In contrast, nurse managers’ and colleagues’ attitudes positively influenced error-reporting intention (β=.613, p<.001). The indirect effect (–.236) was significant, with a 95% bootstrap CI not including zero (–.359 to –.110), confirming a full mediation. These findings highlight that nurses’ error-reporting intention is shaped not directly by patient safety silence but through the attitudes of nurse managers and colleagues. Strengthening leadership support, peer support, and an open communication culture is essential to promote error-reporting behavior.

Meanwhile, Multiple factors contribute to patient safety silence, ranging from individual-level issues such as apathy, lack of self-confidence, or prior experiences with punitive responses, to organizational and cultural influences like prevailing workplace norms, policies, and the broader societal context [8, 9]. Patient safety silence can delay the identification and resolution of system-related problems, potentially leading to serious patient care errors [10].
...
Recent studies suggest that factors such as ethical sensitivity, organizational ethical climate, and—most notably—professional moral courage can help mitigate patient safety silences. These attributes empower nurses to speak up about concerns and prevent adverse events. Cultivating a supportive, ethical environment where nurses feel psychologically safe to disclose errors is essential for reducing patient safety silence and promoting patient safety [7, 11].
...
Meanwhile, despite the growing attention to patient safety in recent decades, the phenomenon of Patient Safety Silence—in which nurses deliberately withhold concerns about safety threats—remains a hidden yet influential barrier to the delivery of safe care [18,19,20, 21]. While organizational factors, such as leadership style and team communication, have been extensively examined, there is limited empirical evidence on the role of individual characteristics, especially professional moral courage, in reducing patient safety silence. Although professional moral courage has been linked to ethical decision-making, whistleblowing, and resilience in challenging situations, its direct impact on nurses’ willingness to speak up about safety threats—especially within local health systems—has not been systematically investigated [18, 21,22,23, 24].
...
This research gap is especially relevant in the Iranian healthcare context, where cultural norms, hierarchical power structures, and fear of blame or punishment often hinder open communication about patient safety risks [25,26, 27]. In such an environment, even nurses who are ethically knowledgeable and professionally competent may hesitate to report unsafe practices. Professional moral courage, in this context, could serve as a key enabler for ethical expression and proactive safety behavior [18, 19, 24]. However, there is a lack of methodologically sound evidence on the relationship between professional moral courage and patient safety silence among Iranian nurses.
...
Previous studies have also confirmed this relationship. Kashani et al. [33] reported a significant positive relationship between safe care and professional moral courage. In a review by Arablarimi et al. [34], professional moral courage was linked to professional errors among nurses that compromise patient safety. Elhihi et al. [35] identified professional moral courage as a main predictor of error reporting and emphasized the importance of an ethical work environment that supports reporting without fear. Similarly, Mohammadi et al. [11] found that both moral sensitivity and professional moral courage are related to safe nursing behaviors. Furthermore, Afshari et al. [36] and Yılmaz et al. [37] reported significant associations between moral sensitivity, professional moral courage, and disclosure of safety concerns. Carlisle et al. [38] attributed improved care quality and safety to nurses with higher professional moral courage, and Jeong et al. [7] found a negative relationship between patient safety silence and nurses’ moral sensitivity.
...
Theoretical frameworks from organizational behavior and safety culture help contextualize these findings. For example, Han et al. [29] found that professional moral courage, as a psychological and ethical capacity, contributes to the establishment of psychological safety in the workplace, enabling staff to report concerns and errors without fear of negative consequences. In this regard, the concept of a Just Culture—which emphasizes accountability alongside support—is particularly relevant. Nurses with professional moral courage are more likely to tolerate environmental pressures and fear of punishment and to advocate for patients’ rights [38,39,40, 41].
...
, may struggle to manage ethical dilemmas and hesitate to report safety concerns [47, 48]. Night shifts, often associated with understaffing, fatigue, and reduced supervision, have been found to decrease the motivation to report safety issues [49, 50]. A high nurse-to-patient ratio and job burnout
...
This study demonstrated that higher professional moral courage is related to reduced patient safety silence among nurses. Additionally, longer work experience, greater job satisfaction, and being male were associated with lower levels of patient safety silence. In contrast, inadequate ethics education, night shifts, excessive workloads, and occupational burnout contributed to an increase of patient safety silence. We recommend that administrators foster professional moral courage, improve work conditions, reduce stress, and create psychologically safe environments that encourage reporting. These findings provide a foundation for evidence-based interventions to improve care quality and reduce adverse outcomes. These interventions can inform policy and managerial efforts aimed at strengthening patient safety culture and supporting nurses’ professional integrity. Future research should use longitudinal or interventional designs to test training programs that strengthen moral courage and reduce patient safety silence.
